newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko defiant as Belarus slips back into crisis.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko defiant as Belarus slips back into crisis.

text.p: Hardline President Alexander Lukashenko and the Belarussian parliament were back on a collision course on Saturday on the eve of a controversial referendum on extending the president's powers.

Lukashenko, comparing deputies to animals in a zoo, said in a television interview he had cancelled his half of a political deal, brokered by neighbouring Russia, after parliament failed to approve it.
He announced that a controversial referendum on Sunday on increasing his powers would be mandatory, and prepared to deliver a television address at 9 p.m. (1900 GMT).
Parliament speaker Semyon Sharetsky, who signed the agreement, accused the president of lying.

"The situation in Belarus is getting worse and tensions are growing. We thought we would be able to calm the storm. But the president wanted and still wants to grab more power by anti- constitutional means," he told a news conference.
Each side blamed the other for the collapse of the agreement, which deputies failed to pass at a late night session on Friday despite two addresses from Lukashenko.
"The referendum will have a mandatory character. I declare this directly since neither the parliament nor the constitutional court has fulfilled the obligations which they took on," Lukashenko said.

He said parliament's failure to pass the deal showed disrespect to everyone involved, including Russia, which hailed the accord as a great success for its diplomacy and for the "community" it formed with Belarus last April.
But Sharetsky dismissed this. "As before, he is using lies to seize power. He had no sympathy with anyone, not even sick Yeltsin and leading Russian politicians," he said.
Lukashenko recalled his visit to parliament, where debates raged all day on Friday and one of his supporters tried to grab the microphone after another deputy called Lukashenko a tyrant.
"Excuse me, but it was like a menagerie," he told a television interviewer. "Three at the back shouting, another one shouting on the left, another one jumping, someone hollering, someone whistling."
The Russians had been kind enough to come to Minsk and mediate in the signing of the agreement, he said, "and then they (the parliament) just threw it in the bin."
It was not clear if Lukashenko had consulted Russia deal but Moscow's ambassador in an interview with Reuters described the situation as "very bad".

"Lukashenko is a wise enough politician to solve his domestic problems by himself but I do not exclude the possibility that Russia will try again to solve this crisis," the ambassador, Igor Saprykin, said.
President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman said on Saturday the president considered Friday's compromise as the first key step in ending the conflict, despite its apparent failure.

"Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) considers there is no need to jump to conclusions. He very much counts on the process of fulfilling the agreement being continued and brought to a conclusion," the spokesman said in Moscow.
Meanwhile the constitutional court in Minsk put off until Tuesday a decision on an attempt by deputies to remove Lukashenko from office by impeachment.

"We have decided to sort out how many signatures have been submitted by deputies and meet again on Tuesday," court deputy president Valery Fadeyev said. "There is some doubt about the case. We will have to carry out checks," he added.
Deputies had submitted more than the required 70 signatures to impeach Lukashenko but some withdrew them after Friday's dawn agreement, negotiated by Russian premier Viktor Chernomyrdin.
A deputy who attended the court session said earlier that one judge was absent and the court was split 5-5 over whether to continue considering the impeachment case.
"The president has scared the judges. Now the court will bear moral responsibility for whatever happens to parliament," the deputy, Alexander Dobrovolsky said.
Lukashenko wants to use the referendum to tighten his grip on rival institutions and extend his term by more than two years -- an idea fiercely opposed by parliament.
Parliament, due to meet again on Tuesday, now faces the risk that Lukashenko will either ignore it or order it dissolved if voters, as expected, approve his constitutional draft.
Western officials and his opponents have observed serious flaws in early voting which began almost two weeks ago on November 9. The situation in Minsk on Saturday remained calm.
